adv_abstract.title: Abstract Classes & Abstraction
adv_abstract.overview: Abstract classes define a template for subclasses. They can contain both abstract methods (no body) and concrete methods, enabling a mix of enforced contracts and shared behaviour.
adv_abstract.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Abstract Class

Declared with abstract; cannot be instantiated directly. Subclasses must implement all abstract methods or also be declared abstract.

abstract class Shape {
    abstract double area();
    void describe() {
        System.out.println("Area: " + area());
    }
}

2. Concrete Subclass

class Circle extends Shape {
    double radius;
    Circle(double r) { this.radius = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}

3. Abstract vs Interface

Use an abstract class when subclasses share state or partial implementation. Use an interface to define a pure contract.

codeExamples.title: Abstract class with concrete helper

keyTakeaways: Abstract classes can have constructors, fields, and concrete methods.
You cannot instantiate an abstract class — only its concrete subclasses.
Abstract methods force subclasses to provide their own implementation.
Prefer abstract classes over interfaces when you need shared state.

adv_interfaces.title: Interfaces & Default Methods
adv_interfaces.overview: Interfaces define pure contracts. Since Java 8 they can also contain default and static methods, enabling API evolution without breaking existing implementations.
adv_interfaces.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Interface Declaration

interface Drawable {
    void draw();
    default String description() { return "A drawable shape"; }
}

2. Multiple Implementation

A class can implement multiple interfaces, granting a form of multiple inheritance for behaviour.

class Icon implements Drawable, Serializable {
    public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing icon"); }
}

3. Functional Interfaces

An interface with exactly one abstract method — the basis for lambda expressions.

@FunctionalInterface
interface Transformer { String transform(String s); }

codeExamples.title: Default method conflict resolution

keyTakeaways: Interfaces can have default and static methods since Java 8.
A class must resolve conflicts when two interfaces provide the same default method.
Functional interfaces enable lambda syntax and method references.
Use interfaces to decouple API from implementation.

adv_generics.title: Generics
adv_generics.overview: Generics allow classes and methods to operate on typed parameters, providing compile-time type safety while eliminating casts.
adv_generics.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Generic Class

class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    Box(T v) { this.value = v; }
    T get() { return value; }
}

2. Bounded Type Parameters

class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
    T value;
    double doubled() { return value.doubleValue() * 2; }
}

3. Wildcards

? extends T (upper bound) for reading; ? super T (lower bound) for writing.

codeExamples.title: Generic method

keyTakeaways: Generics provide type safety at compile time with no runtime overhead.
Use <T extends Foo> to restrict the type parameter to subclasses of Foo.
Wildcards make generic code more flexible: ? extends T for reading, ? super T for writing.
Type erasure means generic type info is removed at runtime.

col_list.title: List — ArrayList & LinkedList
col_list.overview: The List interface models an ordered sequence. ArrayList uses a dynamic array for O(1) random access; LinkedList uses doubly-linked nodes for O(1) add/remove at both ends.
col_list.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Creating a List

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");
names.add("Bob");
System.out.println(names.get(0)); // Alice

2. Common Operations

names.remove("Bob");
Collections.sort(names);
names.forEach(System.out::println);

3. ArrayList vs LinkedList

ArrayList wins for random access; LinkedList wins for frequent insertions/deletions in the middle.

codeExamples.title: Iterating with index and for-each

keyTakeaways: ArrayList.get(i) is O(1); LinkedList.get(i) is O(n).
Use List.of() for immutable lists; new ArrayList<>() for mutable.
Collections.sort() works on any List; provide a Comparator for custom order.
Prefer ArrayList unless you frequently add/remove at arbitrary positions.

col_map.title: Map — HashMap & TreeMap
col_map.overview: Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys. HashMap offers O(1) average-case operations; TreeMap keeps keys sorted and offers O(log n).
col_map.keyConceptsHtml:
1. HashMap basics

Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Alice", 95);
scores.put("Bob", 82);
System.out.println(scores.get("Alice")); // 95

2. Iteration

for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> e : scores.entrySet())
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + " -> " + e.getValue());

3. getOrDefault & putIfAbsent

scores.getOrDefault("Carol", 0); // 0
scores.putIfAbsent("Dave", 70);

codeExamples.title: Word frequency counter

keyTakeaways: HashMap.get/put are O(1) average under low load factor.
TreeMap entries are always sorted by key (natural order or Comparator).
Use merge() or computeIfAbsent() to simplify accumulation patterns.
Keys must properly implement hashCode() and equals().

col_set.title: Set — HashSet & TreeSet
col_set.overview: Set guarantees uniqueness. HashSet offers O(1) add/contains; TreeSet keeps elements sorted.
col_set.keyConceptsHtml:
1. HashSet Usage

Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add("apple");
seen.add("banana");
seen.add("apple"); // duplicate ignored
System.out.println(seen.size()); // 2

2. Set Operations

Set<Integer> a = new HashSet<>(Set.of(1,2,3));
Set<Integer> b = new HashSet<>(Set.of(2,3,4));
a.retainAll(b); // intersection: {2,3}

codeExamples.title: Remove duplicates from a list

keyTakeaways: Sets reject duplicate elements based on equals()/hashCode().
HashSet has O(1) add/contains; TreeSet has O(log n) but sorted.
LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order.
Use Set.copyOf() for an immutable snapshot.

col_queue.title: Queue & Deque
col_queue.overview: Queue models FIFO processing. Deque (double-ended queue) supports insertion and removal at both ends, acting as both queue and stack.
col_queue.keyConceptsHtml:
1. LinkedList as Queue

Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>();
q.offer("first");
q.offer("second");
System.out.println(q.poll()); // first

2. PriorityQueue

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.add(5); pq.add(1); pq.add(3);
System.out.println(pq.poll()); // 1 (min-heap)

3. ArrayDeque as Stack

Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("a"); stack.push("b");
System.out.println(stack.pop()); // b

codeExamples.title: BFS skeleton using Queue

keyTakeaways: Use offer/poll (Queue) instead of add/remove to avoid exceptions on empty queues.
PriorityQueue orders by natural order or custom Comparator.
ArrayDeque is faster than LinkedList for stack/queue use-cases.
Deque can be used as a double-ended queue, queue, or stack.

stream_basics.title: Stream API Basics
stream_basics.overview: The Stream API (Java 8+) provides a declarative pipeline for processing sequences of data with lazy evaluation and optional parallelism.
stream_basics.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Creating Streams

Stream<String> s1 = Stream.of("a","b","c");
Stream<Integer> s2 = List.of(1,2,3).stream();
IntStream range = IntStream.range(0, 5);

2. Lazy Evaluation

Intermediate operations (filter, map) are lazy — they don't execute until a terminal operation (collect, forEach) is called.

3. Terminal Operations

List.of(1,2,3,4).stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 2, 4

codeExamples.title: Collect filtered results

keyTakeaways: Streams are single-use — you cannot reuse a consumed stream.
Intermediate operations are lazy; terminal operations are eager.
Use Collectors.toList(), toMap(), joining() to collect results.
Parallel streams via .parallelStream() — only beneficial for large CPU-bound tasks.

stream_lambda.title: Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces
stream_lambda.overview: Lambdas provide concise anonymous function syntax. Combined with functional interfaces they power the entire Streams and function composition API.
stream_lambda.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Lambda Syntax

// (params) -> expression
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello");
Comparator<String> cmp = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();

2. Method References

List.of("x","y","z").forEach(System.out::println);
List.of(1,2,3).stream().map(String::valueOf).forEach(System.out::println);

3. Built-in Functional Interfaces

  • Predicate<T> — boolean test(T t)
  • Function<T,R> — R apply(T t)
  • Consumer<T> — void accept(T t)
  • Supplier<T> — T get()

codeExamples.title: Compose Predicates

keyTakeaways: A lambda is essentially an instance of a functional interface.
Use :: for method references: ClassName::method or instance::method.
Predicate.and/or/negate allows composing conditions.
Captured local variables must be effectively final.

stream_ops.title: Stream Operations: filter, map, reduce
stream_ops.overview: Core stream operations transform data pipelines: filter selects elements, map transforms them, reduce aggregates them into a single value.
stream_ops.keyConceptsHtml:
1. filter

Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5)
    .filter(n -> n > 2)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 3 4 5

2. map & flatMap

Stream.of("hello","world")
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
Stream.of(List.of(1,2), List.of(3,4))
    .flatMap(Collection::stream)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 1 2 3 4

3. reduce

int sum = Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5)
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum);
System.out.println(sum); // 15

codeExamples.title: Collect to grouped Map

keyTakeaways: filter, map, flatMap are intermediate (lazy); collect, reduce, count are terminal.
flatMap flattens a stream of streams into one stream.
Collectors.groupingBy creates a Map grouping by a classifier function.
reduce requires an identity value and an associative accumulator.

exc_checked.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
exc_checked.overview: Java distinguishes checked exceptions (must be handled or declared) from unchecked exceptions (runtime errors that don't require explicit handling).
exc_checked.keyConceptsHtml:
1. The Hierarchy

  • Throwable
    • Exception (checked if not subclass of RuntimeException)
      • RuntimeException (unchecked)
    • Error (unchecked, system-level)

2. Checked Example

void readFile(String path) throws IOException {
    BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path));
    System.out.println(br.readLine());
    br.close();
}

3. Unchecked Example

int[] arr = new int[3];
arr[5] = 10; // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — unchecked

codeExamples.title: Checked vs unchecked side by side

keyTakeaways: Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException.
The compiler forces you to catch or declare checked exceptions.
Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses) indicate programming bugs.
Errors (OutOfMemoryError etc.) should generally not be caught.

exc_custom.title: Custom Exceptions
exc_custom.overview: Creating domain-specific exception classes makes error handling clearer and enables callers to distinguish different failure modes precisely.
exc_custom.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Custom Checked Exception

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
    private double amount;
    public InsufficientFundsException(double a) {
        super("Insufficient funds: need " + a + " more");
        this.amount = a;
    }
    public double getAmount() { return amount; }
}

2. Exception Chaining

try {
    parseConfig();
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new ConfigException("Failed to load config", e); // wraps original cause
}

codeExamples.title: Using a custom exception

keyTakeaways: Extend Exception for checked or RuntimeException for unchecked custom exceptions.
Always pass a meaningful message to super().
Exception chaining (passing cause to constructor) preserves the original stack trace.
Use custom exceptions to express domain-specific failures clearly.

file_read.title: File I/O — Reading & Writing
file_read.overview: Java provides multiple APIs for reading/writing files. The modern approach uses try-with-resources with BufferedReader/Writer, or the NIO.2 Files utility.
file_read.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Reading with BufferedReader

try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"))) {
    String line;
    while ((line = br.readLine()) != null)
        System.out.println(line);
} // auto-closed

2. Writing with BufferedWriter

try (BufferedWriter bw = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("out.txt"))) {
    bw.write("Hello, file!");
    bw.newLine();
}

3. NIO.2 convenience

Path p = Path.of("data.txt");
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(p);
Files.writeString(p, "content");

codeExamples.title: Copy a file using NIO.2

keyTakeaways: Always use try-with-resources to ensure streams are closed.
BufferedReader/Writer add buffering for better performance.
NIO.2 (java.nio.file) is the modern, simpler file API.
Files.readAllLines() loads all lines into memory — avoid on large files.

file_streams.title: Byte & Character Streams
file_streams.overview: Java I/O is built on a decorator-pattern hierarchy of streams. Byte streams handle raw binary data; character streams handle text with encoding awareness.
file_streams.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Byte Streams

try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("img.png");
     FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream("copy.png")) {
    byte[] buf = new byte[1024];
    int read;
    while ((read = fis.read(buf)) != -1)
        fos.write(buf, 0, read);
}

2. Character Streams

InputStreamReader/OutputStreamWriter bridge byte ↔ char with a specified charset.

Reader r = new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("f.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

3. Object Serialisation

// Serialise
try (ObjectOutputStream oos = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("obj.bin"))) {
    oos.writeObject(myObject);
}

codeExamples.title: Reading a binary file into byte array

keyTakeaways: Byte streams: InputStream/OutputStream — for images, audio, binary data.
Character streams: Reader/Writer — for text, respects charset.
The decorator pattern means you wrap streams for extra capability.
Use ObjectOutputStream/ObjectInputStream for Java object serialisation.

thread_basics.title: Thread Basics
thread_basics.overview: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution. Java threads can be created by extending Thread or implementing Runnable, and share the process memory space.
thread_basics.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Extending Thread

class MyThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Running: " + getName());
    }
}
new MyThread().start();

2. Implementing Runnable

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Lambda thread");
Thread t = new Thread(r);
t.start();
t.join(); // wait for completion

3. sleep & interrupt

try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }

codeExamples.title: Two threads racing

keyTakeaways: Always call start(), not run(), to launch a new thread.
Prefer Runnable over extending Thread to keep concerns separated.
join() blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes.
Catch InterruptedException and restore the interrupted flag.

thread_sync.title: Synchronisation & Locks
thread_sync.overview: When multiple threads access shared mutable state, synchronisation prevents race conditions: only one thread can execute a synchronised section at a time.
thread_sync.keyConceptsHtml:
1. synchronized Method

class Counter {
    private int count = 0;
    public synchronized void increment() { count++; }
    public synchronized int get() { return count; }
}

2. synchronized Block

private final Object lock = new Object();
void update() {
    synchronized (lock) {
        // critical section
    }
}

3. volatile

Ensures visibility of changes across threads without mutual exclusion.

private volatile boolean running = true;

codeExamples.title: ReentrantLock

keyTakeaways: synchronized ensures only one thread executes the critical section at once.
volatile guarantees memory visibility but not atomicity.
ReentrantLock provides tryLock() and timed lock acquisition.
Always release locks in a finally block to avoid deadlocks.

thread_lifecycle.title: Thread Lifecycle & ExecutorService
thread_lifecycle.overview: Threads transition through well-defined states. ExecutorService manages a pool of worker threads, decoupling task submission from thread management.
thread_lifecycle.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Thread States

NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED | WAITING | TIMED_WAITING) → TERMINATED

2. ExecutorService

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task"));
pool.shutdown();

3. Callable & Future

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> 42);
System.out.println(f.get()); // blocks until result ready

codeExamples.title: Parallel sum with Callable

keyTakeaways: Prefer ExecutorService over raw Thread management for scalability.
Use Callable<T> when a task needs to return a value.
Future.get() blocks — use timeout variant to avoid indefinite waits.
Always call shutdown() or shutdownNow() to release thread pool resources.

ds_arrays_lists.title: Arrays & Array-Based Lists
ds_arrays_lists.overview: Array-backed structures store elements in contiguous memory. This gives O(1) random access but O(n) insertion/deletion in the middle.
ds_arrays_lists.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Static Array

int[] arr = new int[10];
arr[0] = 5;
System.out.println(arr.length); // 10

2. Dynamic Array (ArrayList)

Doubles capacity when full — amortised O(1) append.

3. Time Complexity

get(i)O(1)
add(end)O(1) amortised
add(mid)O(n)
remove(mid)O(n)

codeExamples.title: Manual dynamic array resize

keyTakeaways: Arrays provide O(1) random access via index.
Insertion/deletion in the middle requires shifting elements — O(n).
ArrayList doubles its internal array when capacity is exceeded.
Arrays.copyOf() copies elements to a new array of the given length.

ds_stacks_queues.title: Stacks & Queues
ds_stacks_queues.overview: Stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO) are fundamental ADTs implemented efficiently with arrays or linked lists.
ds_stacks_queues.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Stack

Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(1); stack.push(2); stack.push(3);
System.out.println(stack.pop());  // 3 (LIFO)

2. Queue

Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();
queue.offer(1); queue.offer(2); queue.offer(3);
System.out.println(queue.poll()); // 1 (FIFO)

3. Array-backed Circular Buffer

Fixed-size queue implemented with a circular array avoids expensive head-removal shifts.

codeExamples.title: Balanced brackets using Stack

keyTakeaways: Stack: push to top, pop from top — LIFO.
Queue: enqueue at back, dequeue from front — FIFO.
ArrayDeque is the recommended implementation for both in Java.
Circular buffer gives O(1) enqueue and dequeue with fixed memory.

ds_trees.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
ds_trees.overview: Trees are hierarchical structures. A Binary Search Tree maintains an ordering invariant enabling O(log n) average search, insert, and delete.
ds_trees.keyConceptsHtml:
1. BST Property

For every node: left subtree contains smaller keys; right subtree contains larger keys.

2. Traversals

  • In-order (LNR) — yields sorted sequence
  • Pre-order (NLR) — root first
  • Post-order (LRN) — root last

3. Balanced Trees

Unbalanced BSTs degrade to O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n) worst case. Java's TreeMap uses a Red-Black tree.

codeExamples.title: Simple BST node

keyTakeaways: BST search/insert is O(log n) average, O(n) worst case (degenerate).
In-order traversal of a BST yields elements in sorted order.
TreeMap and TreeSet use a Red-Black tree internally.
Prefer TreeMap over sorted iteration over HashMap.

ds_hashing.title: Hash Tables
ds_hashing.overview: Hash tables achieve O(1) average-case lookup, insert, and delete by mapping keys to indices via a hash function and resolving collisions.
ds_hashing.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Hash Function

Maps a key to a bucket index. Java's hashCode() method and % table-size.

2. Collision Resolution

  • Chaining — each bucket holds a linked list of entries.
  • Open addressing — probe for the next empty bucket.

3. Load Factor

When (entries / buckets) exceeds the load factor (default 0.75 in Java), the table is resized and rehashed.

codeExamples.title: Custom hashCode and equals

keyTakeaways: hash + equals contract: equal objects must have identical hashCodes.
Chaining (HashMap default) keeps each bucket as a list.
Load factor controls the resize threshold — lower = faster lookups, more memory.
Always override both hashCode() and equals() together.

algo_sorting.title: Sorting Algorithms
algo_sorting.overview: Sorting is foundational. Comparison-based algorithms have an O(n log n) lower bound. MergeSort, QuickSort, and HeapSort all achieve this.
algo_sorting.keyConceptsHtml:
1. MergeSort

Divide array in half, sort each half recursively, merge. Stable, O(n log n) guaranteed, O(n) extra space.

2. QuickSort

Pick a pivot, partition around it. Average O(n log n), worst O(n²) (bad pivot), in-place, not stable.

3. HeapSort

Build a max-heap, then repeatedly extract max. O(n log n), in-place, not stable.

codeExamples.title: MergeSort in Java

keyTakeaways: No comparison sort can do better than O(n log n) in the worst case.
Arrays.sort() uses DualPivotQuickSort (primitives) or TimSort (objects).
MergeSort is preferred when stability is required.
QuickSort is often fastest in practice due to cache locality.

algo_searching.title: Searching Algorithms
algo_searching.overview: Searching efficiency depends on data organisation. Linear search works on unsorted data in O(n); binary search requires sorted data and runs in O(log n).
algo_searching.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Linear Search

int linearSearch(int[] arr, int target) {
    for (int i=0; i<arr.length; i++)
        if (arr[i] == target) return i;
    return -1;
}

2. Binary Search

int binarySearch(int[] arr, int target) {
    int lo=0, hi=arr.length-1;
    while (lo<=hi) {
        int mid=(lo+hi)/2;
        if (arr[mid]==target) return mid;
        if (arr[mid]<target) lo=mid+1;
        else hi=mid-1;
    }
    return -1;
}

3. Built-in

Arrays.binarySearch(sortedArr, key); // returns index or negative

codeExamples.title: First occurrence binary search

keyTakeaways: Binary search requires sorted input and runs in O(log n).
Arrays.binarySearch returns insertion point (negative) if not found.
HashMap/HashSet give O(1) membership testing — the go-to for search.
Always prefer sorted structures + binary search over repeated linear scan.

algo_complexity.title: Algorithm Complexity — Big O
algo_complexity.overview: Big O notation characterises how algorithm runtime and memory scale with input size, enabling objective comparison of algorithms.
algo_complexity.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Common Classes

O(1)Constant — array index
O(log n)Logarithmic — binary search
O(n)Linear — single loop
O(n log n)Linearithmic — MergeSort
O(n²)Quadratic — nested loops

2. Amortised Analysis

ArrayList.add() is O(1) amortised — occasional O(n) resize is spread over many cheap operations.

3. Space Complexity

Measure extra memory beyond input. MergeSort: O(n) extra; QuickSort in-place: O(log n) stack.

codeExamples.title: Identifying complexity from code

keyTakeaways: Big O describes asymptotic upper bound as input size → ∞.
Drop constants and lower-order terms: O(3n + 5) = O(n).
Amortised O(1) means occasionally expensive but cheap on average.
Always consider both time and space complexity when comparing solutions.

adv_recursion.title: Advanced Recursion
adv_recursion.overview: Advanced recursive patterns include backtracking (systematic exploration of choices), memoisation (caching subproblem solutions), and divide & conquer.
adv_recursion.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Backtracking

Try a choice, recurse, undo if it leads to failure. Classic use: N-Queens, subsets, permutations.

2. Memoisation

Map<Integer,Long> memo = new HashMap<>();
long fib(int n) {
    if (n<=1) return n;
    if (memo.containsKey(n)) return memo.get(n);
    long r = fib(n-1)+fib(n-2);
    memo.put(n,r);
    return r;
}

3. Divide & Conquer

Divide problem into independent subproblems, solve recursively, combine. MergeSort is the canonical example.

codeExamples.title: Generate all subsets (backtracking)

keyTakeaways: Backtracking prunes branches early when a partial solution cannot succeed.
Memoisation converts exponential recursion to polynomial with a cache.
Top-down memoisation = recursion + cache; bottom-up = dynamic programming.
Tail recursion can be optimised to a loop by some JVMs.

adv_design.title: Design Considerations & Robustness
adv_design.overview: Writing correct, robust code requires deliberate design: clear preconditions, defensive checks, meaningful tests, and structured error handling.
adv_design.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Preconditions & Assertions

assert index >= 0 : "Index must be non-negative";
Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name cannot be null");

2. Defensive Programming

Validate inputs at system boundaries. Return Optional instead of null. Make objects immutable when possible.

3. Unit Testing Mindset

Write code that is easily testable: small methods, single responsibility, inject dependencies.

codeExamples.title: Returning Optional instead of null

keyTakeaways: Validate all public method inputs — fail fast with clear messages.
Prefer Optional<T> over returning null to make absent values explicit.
Assertions (assert) are for internal invariants, not user input validation.
Small, single-responsibility methods are easier to test and reason about.
